statements.claim: In her abode in Hastinapura, Kunti awaited news of her sons' plea for peace; Krishna came straight from the assembly of the Kurus, entered, worshipped her feet, and sitting before her laid the whole embassy before her briefly.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.132: 'Entering her abode and worshipping her feet, Kesava represented to her briefly all that had transpired in the assembly of the Kurus.' Location Hastinapura per the pack's index entry.

statements.claim: Both Krishna and the Rishis had spoken words worthy of acceptance and fraught with reason, but Duryodhana accepted none of them; 'their hour is come,' and Krishna asked what he should carry to the Pandavas as her instructions.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.132: 'Diverse words, worthy of being accepted and fraught with reasons, were said both by myself and the Rishis, but Duryodhana accepted them not. As regards Suyodhana and his followers, their hour is come. With thy leave now, I shall speedily repair unto the Pandavas. What should I say unto the Pandavas as thy instructions to them?'

statements.claim: Kunti's opening charge to Yudhishthira: his virtue is decreasing greatly; he should not act vainly like a reader of the Vedas who catches words but not their real meaning; his understanding, affected by the words of the Vedas alone, views virtue only; the Kshatriya was created from the arms of the Brahmana for ruthless deeds and the protection of the people, to depend on the prowess of his own arms.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.132 (Kunti's speech): 'Thy virtue, O son, is decreasing greatly. Do not act vainly... like a reader of the Vedas incapable of catching their real meaning... Thy understanding, affected by only the words of the Vedas, vieweth virtue alone... For all ruthless deeds and for the protection of the people, from his (Brahmana's) arms was created the Kshatriya, who is to depend upon the prowess of his own arms.'

statements.claim: Kunti gives the instance heard from the aged: Vaisravana, gratified, made a gift of the Earth to the royal sage Muchukunda, who refused it, saying he desired sovereignty won by the prowess of arms; Vaisravana was filled with wonder and delight, and Muchukunda ruled the earth, having conquered it by the prowess of his arms.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.132: 'Vaisravana, having been gratified, made a gift of this Earth to the royal sage Muchukunda. The latter without accepting the gift, said, "I desire to enjoy that sovereignty which is won by prowess of arms."... Vaisravana was highly delighted and filled with wonder. King Muchukunda then, fully observing the duties of the Kshatriya order ruled this earth, having conquered it by the prowess of his arms.'

statements.claim: A sixth part of the virtue practised by subjects well protected by their king is obtained by that king; the virtue a king practises confers godhead, sin sends him to hell; the penal code properly applied keeps the four orders to their duties; the king is the cause of the age — he who causes the Krita age enjoys heaven exceedingly, he who causes the Kali age earns sin and resides in hell for countless years; 'the king's sins affect the world, and the world's sins affect him.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.132: 'a sixth part of the virtue, practised by subjects well-protected by the king, is obtained... by the king... conferreth godhead on him, while if he perpetrateth sin, he goeth to hell. The penal code properly applied by the ruler, maketh the four orders adhere to their respective duties... It is the king that createth the Krita, the Treta, or the Dwapara age... the Kali age... earneth sin exceedingly... resideth in hell for countless years. Indeed, the king's sins affect the world, and the world's sins affect him.'

statements.claim: Kunti urges him to observe the kingly duties that befit his ancestry; the conduct he wishes to abide in is not that of a royal sage — one stained by weakness of heart, adhering to compassion and unsteady, never obtains the merit of cherishing subjects with love.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.132: 'Observe thou those kingly duties of thine that befit thy ancestry. That is not the conduct of a royal sage in which thou wishest to abide. Indeed, he that is stained by weakness of heart and adhereth to compassion, and is unsteady, never obtaineth the merit born of cherishing his subjects with love.'

statements.claim: The understanding by which Yudhishthira was acting was never wished for him by Pandu, Kunti, or his grandsire; sacrifice, gift, merit, bravery, subjects and children, greatness of soul, might and energy were what she prayed for him, while well-wishing Brahmanas gratified the gods and the Pitris with Swaha and Swadha for his long life, wealth and children.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.132: 'That understanding according to which thou art now acting was never wished (to thee) by Pandu, or myself, or thy grandsire... sacrifice, gift, merit, and bravery, subjects and children, greatness of soul, and might, and energy, these were always prayed by me for thee. Well-wishing Brahmanas duly worshipped and gratified the gods and the Pitris for your long life, wealth, and children, by adding Swaha and Swadha.'

statements.claim: Whether righteous or not, liberality, gift, study, sacrifice and sway over subjects are to be practised in consequence of one's very birth; though born in a high race her sons are destitute of the means of support and afflicted with misery.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.132: 'The mother and the father, as also the gods always desire for their children liberality and gift and study and sacrifice and sway over subjects. Whether all this be righteous or unrighteous, you are to practise it, in consequence of your very birth... though born in a high race, they are yet destitute of the very means of support, and are afflicted with misery.'

statements.claim: Hungry men approaching a brave and bountiful monarch are gratified and live by his side — 'what virtue can be superior to this?'; a virtuous person on acquiring a kingdom should attach all persons by gift, force, or sweet words; a Brahmana should adopt mendicancy, a Vaisya earn wealth, a Sudra serve the other three.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.132: 'Hungry men, approaching a brave and bountiful monarch, are gratified, and live by his side. What virtue can be superior to this? A virtuous person, upon acquiring a kingdom, should... attach some by gift, some by force, and some by sweet words. A Brahmana should adopt mendicancy; a Vaisya should earn wealth; and a Sudra should serve the other three.'

statements.claim: Mendicancy is forbidden to him and agriculture unsuited; as a Kshatriya he is the protector of all in distress and must live by the prowess of his arms, recovering his lost paternal share of the kingdom by conciliation or by war.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.132: 'Mendicancy, therefore, is forbidden to thee. Nor is agriculture suited to thee. Thou art a Kshatriya and therefore, the protector of all in distress. Thou art to live by the prowess of thy arms. O thou of mighty arms, recover thy paternal share of the kingdom which thou hast lost, by conciliation, or by war.'

statements.claim: Krishna received the words; they would be carried unaltered to the camp at Upaplavya, where Yudhishthira would hear that peace was a luxury he could no longer afford.
statements.evidence: Krishna's destination (the Pandavas at Upaplavya) follows from 5.132 ('I shall speedily repair unto the Pandavas') and the corpus chain (next titles: Krishna departs for Upaplavya); the 'peace as a luxury' gloss is interpretive framing, not a sourceable fact.

notes: Near-verbatim rendition of MBh 5.132 (Kunti-Udyoga); no unsupported or contradicted factual claims.

statements.claim: Kunti drew Krishna into the old story of the conversation between Vidula and her son, saying it behoved him to tell Yudhishthira anything that could be gathered from it or anything more beneficial.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.133: 'In this connection, O chastiser of foes, is cited an old story of the conversation between Vidula and her son. It behoveth thee to say unto Yudhishthira anything that can be gathered from this or anything more beneficial than that.'

statements.claim: Vidula was a high-born dame of great foresight — famous, slightly wrathful, of crooked disposition, devoted to Kshatriya virtues, well-educated, known to all the kings of the earth, and learned in the speeches and instructions of teachers of diverse minds.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.133: 'There was a high-born dame of great foresight, named Vidula. She was famous, slightly wrathful, of crooked disposition, and devoted to Kshatriya virtues. Well-educated, she was known to all the kings of the earth. Of great learning, she had listened to the speeches and instructions of diverse mien.'

statements.claim: One day the princess Vidula rebuked her own son, who after his defeat by the king of the Sindhus lay prostrate with his heart depressed by despair.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.133: 'the princess Vidula, one day, rebuked her own son, who, after his defeat by the king of the Sindhus, lay prostrate with heart depressed by despair.'

statements.claim: Her first words: 'Thou art not my son, O enhancer of the joys of foes. Begotten thou hast not been by myself and thy father!... Without wrath... thou canst not be counted as a man. Thy features betray thee to be a eunuch... Rise, O coward. Do not lie down thus, after thy defeat, delighting all thy foes and grieving thy friends, reft of all sense of honour.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.133: verbatim match with the passage's first rebuke, including 'Sinkest thou in despair as long as thou livest? If thou art desirous of thy own welfare, bear thou the burthen... Do not disgrace thy soul... Abandon thy fears.'

statements.claim: The proverbs: little streams are filled with a small quantity of water, the palms of a mouse with a small quantity, and a coward is soon gratified with small acquisitions; better to perish plucking the fangs of a snake than die miserable like a dog; put forth prowess at the risk of life, wander fearlessly like a hawk, or silently watch foes for an opportunity.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.133: 'Little streams are filled up with only a quantity of water. The palms of a mouse are filled with only a small quantity. A coward is soon gratified, with acquisitions that are small. Rather perish in plucking the fangs of a snake than die miserable like a dog. Put forth thy prowess even at the risk of thy life. Like a hawk that fearlessly rangeth the sky, do thou also wander fearlessly or put forth thy prowess, or silently watch thy foes for an opportunity.'

statements.claim: Do not lie down like a carcass or one smitten by thunder; make thyself known by deeds; never occupy the intermediate, low, or lowest station; blaze up like a well-fed fire, like a brand of Tinduka wood blaze even for a moment, never smoulder like a flameless fire of paddy chaff — better to blaze for a moment than smoke forever.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.133: 'Why dost thou lie down like a carcass or like one smitten by thunder? Rise, O coward, do not slumber after having been vanquished by the foe... Make thyself known by thy deeds. Never occupy the intermediate, the low, or the lowest station. Blaze up (like a well-fed fire). Like a brand of Tinduka wood, blaze up even for a moment, but never smoulder from desire, like a flameless fire of paddy chaff. It is better to blaze up for a moment than smoke for ever and ever.'

statements.claim: No son should be born in a royal race who is either exceedingly fierce or exceedingly mild; achieving every great feat in battle, a brave man is freed from his debt to the Kshatriya order, never disgraces himself, and whether he gains his object or not never indulges in grief.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.133: 'Let no son be born in a royal race, who is either exceedingly fierce or exceedingly mild. Repairing to the field of battle and achieving every great feat that is possible for man to achieve, a brave man is freed from the debt he oweth to the duties of the Kshatriya order. Such a person never disgraceth his own self. Whether he gaineth his object or not, he that is possessed of sense never indulgeth in grief.'

statements.claim: If fall one must, seize the foe by the hips and fall with him; even if one's roots are cut off one should not give way to despair; horses of high mettle put forth all their prowess, and remembering their behaviour he should muster strength and honour and exert himself in raising the race that hath sunk because of him.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.133: 'If fall and sink one must, he should seize the foe by the hips (and thus fall with the foe). Even if one's roots are cut off, he should not yet give way to despair. Horses of high mettle put forth all their prowess for dragging or bearing heavy weights. Remembering their behaviour, muster all thy strength and sense of honour... Exert thyself in raising that race which hath sunk, in consequence of thee.'

statements.claim: He who has not achieved a great feat forming the subject of men's conversation only increases the population; he is neither man nor woman; he whose fame rests not on charity, asceticism, truth, learning and wealth is only his mother's excreta; the mendicant's profession is worthy only of a coward; friends find no happiness in the weak man at whose sight foes are delighted.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.133: 'He that hath not achieved a great feat forming the subject of men's conversation, only increaseth the number of population. He is neither man nor woman. He whose fame is not founded in respect of charity, asceticism, truth, learning and acquisition of wealth, is only his mother's excreta... It behoveth thee not to adopt the idle, wretched, infamous, and miserable profession of mendicancy that is worthy only of a coward. Friends never derive any happiness on obtaining that weak person for a friend, at whose sight foes are delighted.'

statements.claim: Vidula's cry: exiled from their kingdom, driven from home, deprived of enjoyment and destitute of resources, they shall perish from want of the means of life; by bringing forth Sanjaya she has brought forth Kali himself in the shape of a son; let no woman bear such a son; 'do not smoulder. Blaze thou up, effectively displaying thy prowess.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.133: 'Alas, exiled from our kingdom, driven from home, deprived of all means of enjoyment and pleasure, and destitute of resources, we shall have to perish from want of the very means of life! Misbehaving in the midst of those that are good, and the destroyer of thy race and family, by bringing thee forth, O Sanjaya, I have brought forth Kali himself in the shape of a son. Oh, let no woman bring forth such a son... Do not smoulder. Blaze thou up, effectively displaying thy prowess.'

statements.claim: The message for Yudhishthira was plain: a mother's love may take the shape of a fury that will not let her defeated son lie down, and Kunti expected Krishna to repeat Vidula's words.
statements.evidence: Interpretive summary of Kunti's own instruction that the tale be conveyed to Yudhishthira (MBh 5.133 opening); framing, not a separate factual assertion.

notes: Near-verbatim rendition of MBh 5.133 (Vidula-Sanjaya); no unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: For Arjuna, Kunti recalled the celestial voice heard when he was brought forth in the lying-in room while she sat in the hermitage surrounded by ladies: he would rival the deity of a thousand eyes, vanquish all the assembled Kurus, aided by Bhima conquer the whole Earth with fame touching the heavens, slay the Kurus with Vasudeva as ally and recover his lost paternal share, and with his brothers perform three great sacrifices.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.137: 'when thou wert brought forth in the lying-in room and when I was sitting in the hermitage surrounded by ladies, a celestial and delightful voice was heard in the sky, saying, "O Kunti, this thy son will rival the deity of a thousand eyes. This one will vanquish in battle all the assembled Kurus. Aided by Bhima, he will conquer the whole Earth... With Vasudeva as his ally, he will slay the Kurus in battle and recover his lost paternal share in the kingdom... perform three great sacrifices."'

statements.claim: Kunti affirms she never doubted the voice and tells Krishna he knows how steady Vibhatsu, otherwise called Savyasachin, is; if there is righteousness the words will be true and Krishna himself will accomplish it all — 'I bow to righteousness, which is superior to all.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.137: 'thou knowest how steady, in truth, is Vibhatsu, otherwise called Savyasachin... let it be as that (celestial) voice said. If... there is anything like righteousness, those words will be true, for then, Krishna, thou wilt thyself accomplish it all. I do not doubt what that voice said. I bow to righteousness which is superior to all.'

statements.claim: For Bhima the message was: 'The time hath come for that in view of which a Kshatriya lady bringeth forth a son! They that are foremost among men never become cheerless when they have hostilities to wage' — and Krishna knew Bhima's mind, that grinder of foes never pacified until he exterminates his foes.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.137: 'Unto Vrikodara again... "The time hath come for that in view of which Kshatriya lady bringeth forth a son! They that are foremost among men never become cheerless when they have hostilities to wage"--Thou knowest what the state of Bhima's mind is. That grinder of foes is never pacified until he exterminates his foes.'

statements.claim: For Draupadi, daughter-in-law of the high-souled Pandu, the praise: 'O thou that art highly blessed, of noble parentage, endued with great fame, that becoming behaviour which thou always showest towards my sons is, indeed, worthy of thee.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.137: 'say unto the auspicious Krishna of great fame, that daughter-in-law of the high-souled Pandu, who is conversant with the details of every virtue... "O thou that art highly blessed, O thou of noble parentage... that becoming behaviour which thou always showest towards my sons is, indeed, worthy of thee."'

statements.claim: To the sons of Madri: covet more than life the enjoyments acquired by prowess; before their eyes the princess of Panchala was addressed in cruel and abusive epithets; the loss of the kingdom and the defeat at dice grieved her not, but Draupadi weeping in the assembly hearing cruel words grieved her most — exceedingly beautiful Krishna found no protector though wedded to powerful protectors.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.137: 'say unto the sons of Madri... "Covet ye more than life itself, those enjoyments that are acquired by prowess... before your eyes the princess of Panchala was addressed in cruel and abusive epithets... The deprivation of their kingdom grieved me not. Their defeat at dice grieved me not. But that noble and fair Draupadi, however, while weeping in the midst of the assembly, had to hear those cruel and insulting words is what grieveth me most... found no protector on that occasion, though she was wedded to such powerful protectors."'

statements.claim: The final instruction to Arjuna: he should always tread the path pointed out by Draupadi; Bhima and Arjuna, that pair of fierce all-destroying Yamas, could make the gods themselves go the way of all creatures — was it not an insult that their wife was dragged into the assembly? — and Krishna should recall the cruel words Dushasana said to Bhima before all the warriors of Kuru's race.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.137: 'say unto that tiger among men, Arjuna... that he should always tread in the path that may be pointed out by Draupadi... Bhima and Arjuna,--that pair of fierce and all-destroying Yamas, are capable of making the very gods go the way of all creatures. Is not this an insult to them that (their wife) Krishna was dragged into the assembly? O Kesava, recall to their remembrance all those cruel and harsh words that Dussasana said unto Bhima in the very presence of all the warriors of Kuru's race.'

statements.claim: Kunti asked Krishna to enquire after the welfare of the Pandavas with their children and of Draupadi, to say she was well, and bade him go on his auspicious way and protect her sons.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.137: 'Enquire (in my name) after the welfare of the Pandavas with their children and Krishna. Say unto them, O Janardana, that I am well. Go thou on thy auspicious way, and protect my sons!'

statements.claim: Krishna rose, saluted her, walked round her in farewell, and issued out of her abode.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.137 (Vaisampayana): 'Saluting and walking round her, the mighty-armed Krishna whose gait resembled the majestic gait of the lion, then issued out of Pritha's abode.'

statements.claim: He carried his last messages out of the city, and the road to Upaplavya lay open before him.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.137 continuation: Krishna then dismissed the Kuru chiefs with Bhishma at their head, took Karna upon his chariot accompanied by Satyaki, and left the Kuru city; the same passage closes with him reaching Upaplavya.

statements.claim: Krishna's farewell to Kunti comprised parting words for each of her sons and the daughter-in-law she held dear.
statements.evidence: Opening frame counting the chapter's successive messages (Arjuna, Bhima, sons of Madri, Draupadi, and Arjuna again); organizing device, no distortion of the record.

notes: Faithful compression of MBh 5.137 (Kunti's parting messages and Krishna's leave-taking); no issues.

statements.claim: At the edge of the royal quarter Krishna dismissed the chiefs of the Kurus, with Bhishma at their head, who had followed him through the city; then he took Karna upon his chariot, called Satyaki to his side, and drove out through the gates.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.137: 'he then dismissed those chiefs among the Kurus with Bhishma at their head (who had followed him), and taking Karna upon his chariot, left (the Kuru city), accompanied by Satyaki.'

statements.claim: After his departure the Kurus assembled and talked of the wonderful incident connected with him, saying 'Overcome with ignorance, the whole earth hath been entangled in the meshes of death!' and 'Through Duryodhana's folly, all this is doomed to destruction.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.137: 'the Kurus assembled together and began to talk of that highly wonderful and marvellous incident connected with him. And they said, "Overcome with ignorance, the whole earth hath been entangled in the meshes of death!"... "Through Duryodhana's folly, all this is doomed to destruction."'

statements.claim: What passed between Krishna and Karna on the road is not set down in this telling; the source records only that the foremost of persons proceeded deliberating with Karna for a long time, the chariot keeping pace with the conversation.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.137: 'Having issued out of the (Kuru) city, that foremost of persons proceeded, deliberating with Karna for a long time.' The story explicitly disclaims the dialogue's content as belonging to another telling.

statements.claim: When Krishna had said what he came to say he dismissed Karna and urged his steeds to greater speed; Daruka held the reins, and the swift coursers endued with the speed of the tempest of the mind went on as if drinking the skies; traversing a long way like fleet hawks they reached Upaplavya very soon, bearing the wielder of Saranga back to the camp of the Pandavas.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.137: 'that delighter of all the Yadavas then dismissed Karna and urged his steeds to greater speed. And driven by Daruka, those swift coursers endued with the speed of the tempest of the mind, went on as if drinking the skies. And quickly traversing a long way like fleet hawks, they reached Upaplavya very soon, bearing the wielder of Saranga.'

statements.claim: He had come to the Kuru capital as a messenger of peace and the embassy had failed: Duryodhana had refused every word Krishna and the Rishis had spoken, and the earth stood on the edge of war.
statements.evidence: Recap of the immediately preceding chapters in the same corpus chain: MBh 5.132 (Duryodhana accepted nothing; 'their hour is come') and the Kurus' own words in 5.137 ('the whole earth hath been entangled in the meshes of death').

statements.claim: Krishna had come to Hastinapura carrying a secret about Karna's birth, a secret he had chosen this road to begin telling, to be carried to its end on a later road when the charioteer's son would learn who he truly was.
statements.evidence: Narrative positioning that defers the content to the corpus's following stories (DKS_0441-0444, which dramatize the revelation per the pack's corpus chain); no contradictory factual assertion in this telling ('the source records only that... deliberating with Karna for a long time').

statements.claim: The messenger of peace rode in alone, having left behind the one man of the Kuru side he had chosen to ride beside, and a city that already knew itself doomed.
statements.evidence: Closing atmosphere consistent with the source (Karna dismissed, Kurus predicting doom); figurative framing rather than a distinct sourceable fact.

notes: Renders exactly the MBh 5.137 leave-taking tail (same chapter as DKS_0439's pack); the birth-secret paragraph is a frame deferring to later stories, disclaiming its own content. No issues.

statements.claim: On the road outside Hastinapura, Krishna told Karna what no one in that city had told him plainly: Kunti had borne him before her marriage through her union with Surya the sun god; he was her firstborn, the eldest of the Pandavas, older than Yudhishthira himself; and Krishna offered him the kingdom.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.141 (Karna's reply presupposes Krishna's revelation and offer): Karna says 'My mother, while a maiden, bore me in her womb... through her connection with Surya... Morally, I am the son of Pandu,' and warns that if Yudhishthira 'cometh to know me as the firstborn son of Kunti, he will never accept the kingdom,' and that were the empire his he would make it over to Duryodhana; the pack's index summary states Krishna offered him the kingdom.

statements.claim: Karna answered steadily, acknowledging Krishna spoke from love, affection and friendship and a desire to do him good: 'Morally, I am the son of Pandu, as the scriptures hold. My mother, while a maiden, bore me through her connection with Surya, and at Surya's own command she abandoned me as soon as I was born, without thinking of my welfare.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.141: 'thou hast said these words from thy love, affection, and friendship for me, as also in consequence of thy desire of doing me good... Morally, I am the son of Pandu, as also in consequence of the injunctions of the scriptures... My mother, while a maiden, bore me in her womb... through her connection with Surya. And at the command of Surya himself, she abandoned me as soon as I was born... Kunti, however, abandoned me without thinking of my welfare.'

statements.claim: The charioteer Adhiratha found the abandoned child and took him home; Radha's breasts filled with milk that very day, she cleansed and raised him; Adhiratha performed every rite of infancy on him according to the scriptures and had the Brahmanas bestow the name Vasushena; when he came of age Adhiratha chose his wives, and through them his sons and grandsons were born, and all his bonds of affection were fixed on them.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.141: 'The Suta, Adhiratha, as soon as he beheld me, took me to his home, and from her affection for me, Radha's breasts were filled with milk that very day, and she... cleansed my urine and evacuations... Adhiratha... caused all the rites of infancy to be performed on my person, according to the rules prescribed in the scriptures... caused the name Vasushena to be bestowed upon me by the Brahmanas. When also I attained to youth, I married wives according to his selections. Through them have been born my sons and grandsons... My heart also... and all the bonds of affection and love, are fixed on them.'

statements.claim: Karna: 'From joy or fear, Govinda, I cannot break those bonds, not for the whole earth, not for heaps of gold.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.141: 'From joy or fear, O Govinda, I cannot venture to destroy those bonds even for the sake of the whole earth or heaps of gold.'

statements.claim: He had known for years that he was not of the Suta class by birth, and it had changed nothing: with the Sutas he performed his sacrifices and all his family and marriage rites; through friendship with Duryodhana he had enjoyed sovereignty for thirteen years without a thorn at his side.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.141: 'In consequence also of my connection with Duryodhana... I have... enjoyed sovereignty for thirteen years, without a thorn on my side. I have performed many sacrifices, always however in connection with persons of the Suta tribe. All my family rites and marriage rites have been performed with the Sutas.'

statements.claim: It was Duryodhana who, having won him, had prepared for war and provoked hostilities with the Pandavas, and Karna had been chosen as the great antagonist of Arjuna to advance against him in single combat; 'for the sake of death, or the ties of blood, or fear, or temptation, I cannot behave falsely toward the intelligent son of Dhritarashtra. If I do not meet Arjuna in single combat, it will be inglorious for us both.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.141: 'Obtaining me, O Krishna, Duryodhana hath... made this preparations for an armed encounter and provoked hostilities with the sons of Pandu. And it is for this... that in the battle (that will ensue), I... have been chosen as the great antagonist of Arjuna to advance against him in a single combat. For the sake of death, or the ties of blood, or fear, or temptation, I cannot venture... to behave falsely towards the intelligent son of Dhritarashtra. If I do not now engage in a single combat with Arjuna, this will... be inglorious for both myself and Partha.'

statements.claim: Karna asked Krishna to conceal the discourse; if Yudhishthira, virtuous and self-controlled, came to know him as Kunti's firstborn son he would never accept the kingdom; and were the empire his he would make it over to Duryodhana alone — let Yudhishthira be king forever, for he who has Krishna for guide, Arjuna and Bhima for champions, and Nakula, Sahadeva and the sons of Draupadi is fit to rule the whole earth.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.141: 'Thou must, however, conceal this our discourse for the present... If king Yudhishthira, of virtuous soul and well-controlled senses, cometh to know me as the firstborn son of Kunti, he will never accept the kingdom. If, again... this mighty and swelling empire becometh mine, I shall... certainly make it over to Duryodhana only. Let Yudhishthira of virtuous soul become king for ever. He that hath Hrishikesa for his guide, and Dhananjaya and... Bhima for his combatants, as also Nakula and Sahadeva, and the sons of Draupadi, is fit... to rule over the whole earth.'

statements.claim: Karna recited the great warriors of the Pandava host — Dhrishtadyumna of the Panchalas, the mighty Satyaki, Chekitana, the invincible Sikhandin, the Kekaya brothers, Kuntibhoja with his rainbow-colored steeds, and Krishna himself like an ocean — knowing the kingdom celebrated among all the kings of the earth was already won in all but name, and that he would stand against it anyway.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.141: 'Dhrishtadyumna, the prince of the Panchalas, that mighty car-warrior Satyaki... Chekitana, the invincible Sikhandin, the Kekaya brothers... Kuntibhoja... possessed of steeds endued with the colours of the rainbow... and thyself, O Janardana, like an ocean,--great is this assemblage... of Kshatriyas... This blazing kingdom, celebrated among all the kings of the earth, is already won (by Yudhishthira).'

statements.claim: Krishna did not argue: the offer had been made in good faith and refused in good faith, and there was nothing left to say on that road.
statements.evidence: Scene commentary consistent with the pack's excerpt, in which the dialogue continues through the sacrifice prophecy and parting; not itself a sourceable event claim.

statements.claim: As Krishna turned his chariot back toward the city, Karna stood in the dust and watched him go, a man who had refused a kingdom to keep his word.
statements.evidence: The record has Krishna bound for Upaplavya, not back toward Hastinapura: MBh 5.137 tail (same scene) has him 'dismissed Karna and urged his steeds to greater speed... reached Upaplavya very soon,' and MBh 5.147 opens 'Coming back to Upaplavya from Hastinapura... Kesava represented unto the Pandavas all that had happened.' Moreover this scene is not yet over at this point in the source — the discourse continues with the sacrifice prophecy and omens, and only at its end (MBh 5.143) does Karna, 'Dismissed by Kesava... descend from the car.'

statements.claim: In a single afternoon Karna had been given the truth of his birth and the crown of the world, and he had answered with the life he had actually lived.
statements.evidence: Retrospective framing of the dialogue's significance; the 'single afternoon' is story pacing, not a sourceable temporal claim.

corrections.original_sentence: As Krishna turned his chariot back toward the city, Karna stood in the dust and watched him go, a man who had refused a kingdom to keep his word.
corrections.suggested: As Krishna urged his chariot on toward Upaplavya, Karna stood in the dust and watched him go, a man who had refused a kingdom to keep his word.

notes: Faithful to MBh 5.141 through the refusal, loyalty pledge and secrecy request; one contradicted close: Krishna heads for Upaplavya (5.137 tail / 5.147), never back toward the city, and the discourse in fact continues (5.141-143).

statements.claim: Karna told Krishna plainly that the words had been spoken for his good and that the Pandavas, obedient to Krishna, would do all that Krishna had said.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.141: 'Without doubt, O slayer of Madhu, thou hast told me all this for doing me good. The Pandavas also, obedient as they are to thee, will, without doubt, do all that thou hast said.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana was preparing a great sacrifice of arms, in which Krishna himself would stand as the Upadrashtri and hold the office of Adhyaryu.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.141: 'a great sacrifice of arms is about to be celebrated by Dhritarashtra's son. Thou, O Janardana, wilt be the Upadrashtri of that sacrifice. The office of Adhyaryu also, O Krishna, in that sacrifice, will be thine.'

statements.claim: The ape-bannered Arjuna accoutred in mail would be the Hotri; Gandiva the sacrificial ladle; the prowess of the warriors the clarified butter; the celestial weapons Arjuna would release — Aindra, Pasupata, Brahma, Sthunakarna — the mantras; and Abhimanyu, resembling or excelling his father, the chief Vedic hymn.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.141: 'The ape-bannered Vibhatsu accoutred in mail will be the Hotri (his bow), Gandiva will be the sacrificial ladle, and the prowess of the warriors will be the clarified butter... The weapons called Aindra, Pasupata, Brahma, and Sthunakarna, applied by Arjuna, will... be the mantras... Resembling his father, or perhaps, excelling him in prowess, Subhadra's son (Abhimanyu) will be the chief Vedic hymn to be chanted.'

statements.claim: When mighty Bhima struck Duryodhana down, the sacrifice of Dhritarashtra's son would be concluded.
statements.evidence: Pack's source excerpt for MBh 5.141: 'When mighty Bhimasena will slay Duryodhana, then, O Madhava, will this sacrifice of Dhritarashtra's son be concluded' (passage continues past the pack's cut-off).

statements.claim: Karna asked only that Krishna conceal the discourse, for therein lay their benefit — if Yudhishthira ever learned the truth of his birth, the king would never accept the kingdom — and made one further request: 'Bring Kunti's son before me for battle.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.141: 'Thou must, however, conceal this our discourse for the present... Therein lies our benefit... If king Yudhishthira... cometh to know me as the firstborn son of Kunti, he will never accept the kingdom'; pack excerpt: 'bring Kunti's son (Arjuna) before me for battle, keeping for ever this our [discourse secret]'.

statements.claim: All his life Karna had used the words 'Kunti's son' of Arjuna; now he had just learned that he himself was Kunti's son, the firstborn, older than the man he was asking to meet, and he did not take the revelation back or trade it for the kingdom.
statements.evidence: Reflective commentary on the dramatic irony just established in the story's own scene (Karna's 'firstborn son of Kunti' in 5.141); interpretation rather than a distinct sourceable claim.

statements.claim: Krishna listened to the whole prophecy without interrupting; Karna had looked at the coming catastrophe and found in it a shape, and he was asking Krishna to witness, not to save him.
statements.evidence: Framing of the scene ('Krishna did not argue' / silent witness); consistent with the source excerpt ending in Karna's own request; no counter-factual asserted.

notes: Accurate rendering of the sacrifice-of-arms prophecy and secrecy request from MBh 5.141; no issues.

statements.claim: Having heard Krishna's beneficial and auspicious words, Karna worshipped the slayer of Madhu and answered: 'Knowing everything, why do you still seek to beguile me?'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.143: 'Hearing these beneficial and auspicious words of Kesava, Karna worshipped Krishna, the slayer of Madhu, and said these words, "Knowing (everything), why dost thou yet, O thou of mighty arms, seek to beguile me?"'

statements.claim: Karna said the destruction of the whole earth was at hand, for its causes were Sakuni, Dussasana, and king Duryodhana; a great and fierce battle was coming between Pandavas and Kurus that would cover the earth with bloody mire, and all the kings and princes following Duryodhana, consumed by the fire of weapons, would proceed to the abode of Yama.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.143: 'The destruction of the whole earth that is at hand for its cause, Sakuni, and myself, and Dussasana, and king Duryodhana... Without doubt... a great and fierce battle is at hand between the Pandavas and the Kurus which will cover the earth with bloody mire. All the kings and princes following the lead of Duryodhana, consumed by the fire of weapons will proceed to the abode of Yama.' (Story condenses by omitting Karna's self-inclusion in the list of causes — the three it names are all in the source.)

statements.claim: The omens: Saturn afflicting Rohini; Mars wheeling toward Jyeshtha and Anuradhas, sign of a great slaughter of friends; the planet Mahapat lying heavy on Chitra; the spot on the moon's disc shifted; Rahu approaching the sun; meteors falling with loud noise and trembling; elephants crying frightfully and horses shedding tears, refusing food and drink.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.143: 'Sanaischara (Saturn), is afflicting the constellation called Rohini... Angaraka (Mars), wheeling... towards the constellation Jeshthya, approacheth towards Anuradhas, indicating a great slaughter of friends... the planet Mahapat afflicteth the constellation Chitra. The spot on the lunar disc hath changed its position; and Rahu also approacheth towards the sun. Meteors are falling from the sky with loud noise and trembling motion. The elephants are sending forth frightful cries, while the steeds... are shedding tears, without taking any delight in food and drink.'

statements.claim: In every division of Duryodhana's army soldiers ate little and passed much — a defect in the eyes of the wise — while the elephants and steeds of the Pandavas were cheerful and the animals wheeled to their right, an omen of success; the same animals passed to the left of Duryodhana's army and incorporeal voices were heard over their heads.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.143: 'amongst the steeds, elephants and soldiers, in all the divisions of Duryodhana's army... while small is the food these take, ample is the excreta they evacuate. The wise have said that this is an indication of defect. The elephants and steeds of the Pandavas... all seem to be cheerful, while all the animals wheel along their right. This also is an indication of their success. The same animal... pass by the left side of Duryodhana's army, while incorporeal voices are constantly heard (over their heads).'

statements.claim: Auspicious birds — peacocks, swans, cranes — followed the Pandavas, while vultures, kankas, hawks, wolves and bees followed the Kauravas; the drums in Duryodhana's camp yielded no sound while those of the Pandavas sounded unstruck; the wells in the Kaurava encampment roared like bulls; the gods showered flesh and blood on Duryodhana's soldiers; vapoury edifices with high walls and porches appeared in the sky over their camp; a black circle surrounded the solar disc; both twilights were terrible and the jackals yelled.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.143: 'All auspicious birds, such as peacocks, swans, cranes... follow the Pandavas, while vultures, Kankas, hawks... wolves and bees... follow the Kauravas. The drums in the army of Dhritarashtra's son yield no sounds, while those of the Pandavas yield sounds without being struck. The wells in the midst of Duryodhana's encampment send forth loud roars like those of huge bulls... The gods are showering flesh and blood... on Duryodhana's soldiers. Vapoury edifices of great effulgence with high walls, deep trenches, and handsome porches, are suddenly appearing in the skies... A black circle surrounding the solar disc appears... Both twilights at sunrise and sunset indicate great terrors. The jackals yell hideously.'

statements.claim: Birds with one wing, one eye and one leg cried out in the dark; fierce birds with black wings and red legs hovered over the camp at nightfall; Duryodhana's soldiers had begun to hate the Brahmanas first, then their preceptors, then their servants; the eastern horizon was red, the southern the hue of weapons, the western earthy, and all the quarters around the encampment seemed ablaze — 'in all these portents great is the danger that is indicated.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.143: 'Diverse birds, each having but one wing, one eye, and one leg, utter terrible cries... Fierce birds with black wings and red legs hover over the Kuru encampment at nightfall... The soldiers of Duryodhana betray hatred for Brahmanas first, and then for their preceptors, and then for all their affectionate servants. The eastern horizon... appeareth red; the southern of the hue of weapons; and western... of an earthy hue. All the quarters around Duryodhana's encampment seem... to be ablaze. In the appearance of all these portents, great is the danger that is indicated.'

statements.claim: The vision: Yudhishthira ascending with his brothers a palace supported by a thousand columns, in white robes and white head-gear, seated on white seats; Krishna enveloping the blood-dyed earth with weapons; Yudhishthira standing on a heap of bones gladly eating buttered payasa from a golden cup and swallowing the earth Krishna handed him — meaning he would rule it; and Bhima, fierce Vrikodara, standing on a summit with mace in hand devouring the earth — meaning he would slay them all in battle.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.143: 'I have in a vision... beheld Yudhishthira ascending with his brothers a palace supported by a thousand columns. All of them appeared with white head-gears and in white robes... seated on white seats... thou... wast beheld by me to be employed in enveloping the blood-dyed earth with weapons. Yudhishthira... ascending upon a heap of bones, was gladly eating buttered payasa of a golden cup. I further beheld Yudhishthira... swallowing the earth handed over to him by thee. This indicates that he will verily rule the earth. I beheld that tiger among men, Vrikodara, of fierce deeds, standing on the summit, mace in hand, and as if devouring this earth. This plainly indicates that he will slay all of us in fierce battle.'

statements.claim: Krishna's answer: 'Indeed, the destruction of the earth is at hand, when my words do not become acceptable to your heart.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.143 pack excerpt: 'Indeed, the destruction of the earth is at hand when my words, O Karna, do not become acceptable to thy heart.'

statements.claim: Karna pressed Krishna to his bosom, holding him once as a man holds a friend he may never see again; dismissed by Kesava, he descended from the chariot, and the two parted on the road.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.143 pack excerpt: 'Having spoken these words, Karna closely pressed Madhava to his bosom. Dismissed by Kesava, he then descended from the car.' (The 'friend he may never see again' simile is connective colour on the source action.)

notes: Comprehensive, near-verbatim rendering of MBh 5.143 (omens, visions, and parting); the story drops Karna's self-inclusion among the causes of destruction ('and myself') but asserts nothing false. No issues.

statements.claim: Krishna's chariot rolled into Upaplavya; he told the Pandavas everything that had happened at Hastinapura, sat long in consultation with them, and then, wearied, went to his own quarters for rest.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.147: 'Coming back to Upaplavya from Hastinapura, that chastiser of foes, Kesava, represented unto the Pandavas all that had happened, and conferring with them for a long space of time, and holding repeated consultations, Sauri went to his own quarters for rest.'

statements.claim: The Pandavas dismissed the kings gathered around them, with Virata at their head; when the sun had set they said their evening prayers with hearts fixed on Krishna, then brought him into their midst and deliberated again.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.147: 'dismissing all the kings, with Virata and others at their heads, the five brothers--the Pandavas--when the sun had set, said their evening prayers. And with hearts ever fixed on Krishna they began to think of him. And, at last, bringing Krishna of Dasarha's race into their midst, they began to deliberate again about what they should do.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira asked Krishna: 'O you of lotus-petal eyes, tell us all that you said to Dhritarashtra's son in the assembly of the Kurus.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.147: 'Yudhishthira said, "O thou of eyes like lotus-petals, it behoveth thee to tell us all that thou saidst unto Dhritarashtra's son in the assembly (of the Kurus), having gone to Nagapura." (The source's Nagapura is rendered Hastinapura, its conventional identity in this narrative.)

statements.claim: Krishna answered briefly: 'Having gone to the city of Hastinapura, I addressed Dhritarashtra's son in the assembly with words that were true, reasonable, and beneficial. That wicked-minded fellow did not accept them.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.147: 'Having gone to Nagapura, I addressed Dhritarashtra's son in the assembly such words as were true, reasonable, and beneficial. That wicked minded fellow did not, however, accept them.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira pressed for the full account: what did the aged grandsire Bhishma, the preceptor Drona son of Bharadwaja, his parents Dhritarashtra and Gandhari, their junior father Kshattri (Vidura) — foremost of those who know virtue, always afflicted with sorrow for them, regarding them as his sons — and all the assembled kings say; the disagreeable words of the Kuru chiefs had flitted from his memory, and Krishna was their refuge, lord and guide.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.147: 'When Duryodhana desired to tread along the wrong path, what did the aged Kuru grandsire say... What also did the highly-blessed preceptor--the son of Bharadwaja, say? And what did his parents Dhritarashtra and Gandhari say? What did our junior father Kshattri, who is the foremost of all persons conversant with virtue, and who is always afflicted with sorrow on account of ourselves whom he regards as his sons, say...? What also did all the kings who sat in that assembly say?... Thou hast already told us all the disagreeable words that the Kuru chiefs... said... Those words, however... have flitted away from my memory... Thou, O Krishna, art our refuge, thou art our lord, thou art our guide!'

statements.claim: Krishna began his recounting: 'Hear, O king, the words that were addressed to Duryodhana in the midst of the assembly of the Kurus, and bear them in mind. After my words were ended, Dhritarashtra's son laughed aloud.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.147: 'Hear, O king, the words that were addressed to king Suyodhana in the midst of the assembly of the Kurus, and, O king of kings, bear them in thy mind. After my words were ended, Dhritarashtra's son laughed aloud.'

statements.claim: Highly incensed, Bhishma rose and spoke for the preservation of their race: for his father Santanu's sake he had procured Kali to become his mother and renounced the throne, so that an only son might not be the end of the line; Vichitravirya was born and installed as king while Bhishma served under him; when Vichitravirya died and anarchy seized the realm, the chief of the gods withheld rain until the starving subjects, afflicted with frightful maladies, begged Bhishma to take the throne — and he had refused, keeping his vow.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.147 (Bhishma): 'my father Santanu... I was, at first, his only son... Let not my race be extinct... I procured Kali to become my mother, having myself made a promise highly difficult to observe, for the sake of my father as also for the sake of our race... In her... was born my younger brother... Vichitravirya... I installed Vichitravirya as a ruler of the kingdom, that was mine, while I placed myself under him as a servant of his... Upon his death, there was anarchy in the kingdom and the chief of the gods poured not a drop of rain (on the realm). The subjects then, afflicted by fear of hunger, hastened to me and said, "Be thou our king... Thy subjects are being greatly afflicted by severe and frightful maladies..." ... my heart was undisturbed. Remembering the behaviour of good, I desired to maintain my vow.'

statements.claim: The line Bhishma had sacrificed his kingship to preserve was being led toward ruin by the very prince who carried it.
statements.evidence: Transitional summary of Bhishma's hortatory purpose ('what I say for (the preservation of) our race'), which the pack's passage establishes before the excerpt is cut; no counter-factual asserted.

statements.claim: The night stretched on while Krishna carried that assembly into the quiet camp — the laughter, the anger, the pleadings of parents, preceptor and grandsire — and the Pandavas knew in full what they had known in outline: nothing remained to be said about peace.
statements.evidence: Closing frame consistent with 5.147's structure (Vasudeva's long reported speech follows, of which the pack shows the opening); atmosphere and anticipation, not a separate sourceable claim.

notes: Faithful to MBh 5.147 (return to Upaplavya, Yudhishthira's request, Krishna's summary, opening of Bhishma's speech); no issues. Nagapura/Hastinapura gloss is standard for this passage.
